title: Write the packager for an EBCDIC link from its samples

blocks.text: A new card-network link is booked for certification next week. Its specification lists the fields of an authorization and gives sample messages as hex dumps; the certification analyst will compare your messages with those samples, byte for byte.

`src/main/java/com/example/practice/MastercardLayout.java` builds a `GenericPackager` from a list of field definitions. Finish `fields()`, which returns one `<isofield .../>` element per field, so that the packager writes messages the way the samples do. About ten lines.
One of its samples, an `0200` with fields 3, 4, 11, 41 and 49:
The tests pack other messages and compare them with the specification's other samples.

cases.says: an authorization packs with its MTI written as the samples write it, and unpacks to the same fields
the bitmap goes out as 8 binary bytes, not as 16 EBCDIC hex characters, so the first field follows at byte 12
the PAN and its two-digit length are EBCDIC characters, one byte a digit, not BCD as on a BASE I link
text fields are EBCDIC and filled with EBCDIC spaces (40), not left in ASCII as iso87binary declares them

origin.section: 6.2. A Packager That Reads Its Own Messages Back Proves Nothing

concepts: On a Mastercard-style link the MTI, numbers, length prefixes and text are one EBCDIC byte each and only the bitmap is binary, so a BCD packager's MTI can't be read.
A wrong field class packs and unpacks its own bytes, so only a comparison with the specification's sample bytes catches it.
